frontmatter.title: How Learning Rate Shapes the Training Curve of a Small CNN
frontmatter.subtitle: One CNN, four learning rates, everything else held fixed

children.value: If you only get to tune one hyperparameter, most people will tell you to tune the learning rate. I wanted to see what that advice looks like in practice. So I took one small CNN, trained it four times on Fashion-MNIST, and changed nothing between the runs except the learning rate.
How does the learning rate change the training and validation curves of a small CNN, and where does it go from “too slow” to “broken”?

Short answer: across a 1000× range, I got everything from a network that was still crawling after 20 epochs, to one that hit 80% validation accuracy in two epochs, to one that gave up completely and guessed at random.
What the learning rate actually does

A real network’s loss surface has millions of dimensions with different curvature in each, but the same three regimes still show up roughly. My experiment looks for them on a real model.

children.value: 10,000 training and 5,000 validation images, both drawn from the official 60k training set. The 10k test set was held out.
2 conv layers (16 and 32 channels, 3×3, ReLU, max-pool) + dense layer of 64 + output layer. 105,866 parameters.
Plain SGD: no momentum, no weight decay, no learning-rate schedule
Laptop CPU, about 25–45 seconds per run
I used a subset so each run takes under a minute on a CPU. The learning rates are spaced by factors of 10 because their effect works on orders of magnitude.
To make the comparison fair, every run starts from
the same batches in the same order

torch.manual_seed(SEED)                              # identical starting weights
model = SmallCNN()
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)     # the one thing that changes
order = torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)          # identical batch order
After each epoch I record training loss, validation loss and validation accuracy. I picked the best learning rate using
accuracy only. I then evaluated that single model on the test set once, at the end. Full code:

Figure 3 puts training and validation loss side by side. At

children.html: η=0.001\eta = 0.001η=0.001

children.value: the two lines overlap, so the model is still underfitting. At

children.html: η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1

children.value: a gap opens up: by epoch 19 training loss is 0.162 and validation loss is 0.348, so the model is starting to fit details of the training set that don’t generalize.
The small rate was stable but slow, the middle rates converged, and the largest broke training. As the parabola suggests, the best value I tried (0.1) sat just below one that failed (1.0).
Divergence looked different than I expected.

children.value: curve swings by about 6 points between neighbouring epochs in mid-training. For example, it drops from 85.5% at epoch 5 to 79.5% at epoch 6. Each SGD step uses only 64 images, so every step contains some noise. A larger learning rate amplifies that noise. Both

η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1

children.value: also drop sharply at epoch 20: 0.1 falls from 88.6% to 75.5%. The two runs saw exactly the same batches, so I suspect the last few batches of epoch 20 pulled both models the same wrong way. I haven’t tested that. The practical lesson is that choosing by
accuracy would have made 0.1 and 0.01 look tied at about 75.5%. Keeping the best validation checkpoint avoids that trap.
Given how noisy the curves are, differences of a point or two between runs are not reliable. Repeating with 3–5 seeds and plotting the mean would fix this.

children.html: η=0.001\eta = 0.001η=0.001

children.value: run was clearly not finished. With enough epochs it would likely close part of the gap, so “worse” here partly means “slower”.
I only tried powers of 10. The real best value could be anywhere between 0.1 and 1.0.
Momentum, Adam or a learning-rate schedule (shrinking

children.html: η\etaη

children.value: over time) would all change where the sweet spot is. A schedule would probably also smooth out the late-epoch swings.
Search the learning rate on a log scale first.
With nothing else changed, moving from 0.001 to 0.1 took best validation accuracy from 72.5% to 88.6%. Try 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, then refine around the best one.
Look at the curve, not just the final number.
A flat loss stuck at ln(number of classes) means the network has stopped learning, often from dead ReLUs. A curve that keeps falling slowly means your rate is probably too small.
With a large learning rate, keep the best checkpoint.
Validation accuracy can swing by several points from one epoch to the next. Selecting on the best validation epoch, not the last one, gives a fairer comparison.
